utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, on Thursday, the 2nd of July, 2015, the Trial Chamber asked us to identify any evidence that the Prosecution intends to lead which might be outside of the scope of the decision on the motion to reopen. I'm about to do so; that is, to identify some Jakarina Kosa-related evidence which was not initially encompassed by Dr. Tabeau's expert report and annexes. These documents that I will be introducing set out Dr. Tabeau's analysis of ICMP DNA identification material regarding the individuals -- the identified individuals exhumed from the Jakarina Kosa mass grave who are not reassociated to the Tomasica mass grave. Now, I've spoken to Mr. Ivetic this morning and agreed that because of the nature of these issues this would be best addressed as a preliminary matter. This document also reflects information related to place and date of disappearances and are marked with 65 ter 32714, 32738, and 32739, which I will be introducing with the witness. The Prosecution provided these data to the Defence as soon as it was received in advance of the testimonies of Dr. Parsons and Dr. Clark, both of whom were also cross-examined about Jakarina Kosa. And while -- the Prosecution submits that these documents are relevant, probative, and reliable, and consequently appropriate for admission into evidence. Also in light of the direct link between Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa, you know, the relevance of this document is -- is clear, and we submit that for these reasons this document should be admitted into evidence. Now, Your Honours, also with regard to the objections and rulings of last Thursday with regard to the evidence that the Prosecution was allowed to lead, we also understand that these documents, these new documents on Jakarina Kosa, are the only instance in which the Prosecution might lead evidence -- is leading evidence which may be outside the scope of the decision on the motion to reopen as we understood your previous ruling related to the evidence presented so far with Dr. Tabeau concerning -- well, we understand your previous ruling reflecting the fact that the evidence was permissible in light of the relief requested by the Prosecutor, and we understand the -- we understood the limitation being referred to only one of the conclusions that the witness made at I believe it's page 45 her report where she -- you know, her conclusions about the fate of the Tomasica-related identified missing -- missing persons was, of course, was her opinion, she was expressing a probability, and the Chamber reassured that this would be not be considered as an established fact. And so I also wanted to place -- also I wanted to place, you know, the discussion of these three additional documents within the context of also the objections and the rulings of last week, and I understand from that Mr. Ivetic that with regard to these three documents, the Defence wouldn't have specific objections about. I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's for three documents. I'm a little confused by what we've just heard now, that the conclusions at page 45 of the report are the witness's opinion and that the Chamber would not consider it as an established fact. I believe Your Honours' ruling was that you would not consider it at all because, of course, as an expert witness an opinion is -- calling something an opinion is dangerous for an expert witness. I think we established that she could not support that opinion as being established and that we were not going to consider that part of her testimony at all, so I'm a little confused now by someone saying it's an opinion. I never once thought it wasn't an opinion. The expert report is presented as an expert opinion and we objected to that part and we received the ruling of the Chamber on that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our understanding was that the ruling was related to the way the Chamber will consider this conclusion, and the Chamber reassured that this was not going to be considered an as established fact but our understanding was that -- wasn't that this -- this portion would be stricken from the -- from the record. From the evidence that Dr. Tabeau presented so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can say on the Defence we had the opposite view, that we thought that Your Honours had excluded that portion of her report from consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, like -- you stated this point at least in two or three occasions, meaning that these -- that that part will not be considered an established fact, but that was the extent of the ruling that we understood, and it was repeated at least three times on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers the matter to be mainly semantics. We said a probability is not an established fact. As short as that. And that still is the position of the Chamber. Now, there's no reason to strike anything from the record. We just explained how the Chamber understood what a probability is, which is not something that has been established as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently is the matter that kept the parties apart. I don't think that the Chamber needs to give any further ruling on the matter as matters stand now. I thank the parts for their submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, then, is that -- is that conclusion by Madam Tabeau in her report an expert opinion that I now need to rebut in my Defence case that goes beyond Tomasica? That's, I think, the crux of the question. So I think Your Honours do need to clarify your ruling. I would ask that you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you mean to say that you have to establish that it's not a probability?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. If Your Honours rule that something is an opinion of an expert witness, then that is something the Defence has to rebut. Since Dr. Tabeau is not here as a fact witness, if she has a conclusion that is her opinion, I need to know whether this Chamber considers it an expert opinion I need to rebut or whether it's something I don't need to address in my cross. Given that when I objected to it three times, you left me with the impression that we were not going to consider it, and now I don't know whether you're going consider it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I remember Mr. Ivetic's objections as being related to the fact he was concerned that that portion would be considered an established fact. So that was the extent of his objection. And Your Honours gave -- Your Honours, the ruling on all this would be considered, that is, not as an established fact. But that was the extent of his objection, as I see it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's now how I remember my own objection, but I stand by what's in the transcript and the fact that I would not have needed to have object if it was just a matter of what we quantify that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could I read to you what you said, Mr. Ivetic. You refer to her words, and those were: "'... thus, these persons likely died in the same events.'" I then said: "Likely died. That's not a fact." You then said: "Well, as -- my goal is make sure that no one can misread it as a fact and conclude otherwise." This observation, this expression of likelihood, which I think is also not directly based on -- I think any factual basis for any opinion that would go further is missing. I think that's what Ms. Tabeau explained to us. And your goal, Mr. Ivetic, to make sure that no one can misread it as a fact, I think that goal is achieved, and that's what you said. And you said that: "... we cannot rely upon her report, that might resolve the issue. But we need to make sure that a majority of Judges agree." And I think on what you were seeking that it was not a fact, even Judge Moloto confirmed that, you would have heard him, and this Chamber considers an expression of likelihood not to be a fact of what is presented as likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add one sentence. The word "opinion" was not used at all during that discussion. In the entire transcript of that day, the word "opinion" was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The Prosecution used the word "opinion" today, which is why I rose because it's the first time we're introducing the word opinion, that someone is quantifying that as an opinion which is what raises my concern because now all of a sudden it's being presented as an expert opinion, whereas yesterday we're talking about whether it was an established fact or not. So I think we're -- the Prosecution is trying to broaden what we discussed yesterday -- what we discussed on Thursday, which was the established fact, and now it's being presented as opinion which creates add knew dilemma because an expert presenting an opinion is something that the Defence needs to rebut because that's something that the Chamber can rely upon. So now I think we need a new ruling based upon now this re-quantification by the Prosecution of as it opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters clear. We should clearly distinguish between likelihood and between a fact. The Chamber has clearly expressed that it doesn't take what was written in the report for a fact. Now, if you want to start a battle with Ms. D'Ascoli on how likely or not likely it is, I think for that likelihood there is not much factual basis, and it's not presented as a likelihood established by the expertise of Ms. Tabeau but just kind of an interpretation on a personal basis. And in cross-examination, of course, you could further explore that. Mr. Ivetic, you were seeking the opinion of the three Judges, and you got it. Therefore, at this moment there's no further need for a ruling, and you may further explore the basis for what Ms. Tabeau said was likely in cross-examination. And the Chamber again stresses that what is considered to be likely in this respect is not considered as a fact and the likelihood is not supported by a -- by anything more than what Ms. Tabeau told us. That is, I think -- but I leave it to that. Having dealt with this, any further matter, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We're ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. But meanwhile, I'll also read a very short decision. On the 30th of June of this year, the Defence has filed two urgent motions seeking the addition of documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. One seeking the addition of 12 documents for use with witness with Simo Tusevljak and another seeking the addition of 21 documents for use with Witness Milutin Misic. On 1st and the 2nd of July, respectively, the Prosecution stated that it did not object to the motions, and this can be found at transcript pages 36574 and 36694. The Chamber finds that the documents at issue are prima facie relevant and probative and that it's in the interest of justice for these documents to be added to the Defence's exhibit lists, and for these reasons the Chamber grants both motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli will now continue her examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could I please have P7453, marked for identification, on the screens please. Dr. Tabeau, while this is coming up, we concluded last week with slide 16 of your presentation summarising some of your findings. I will now continue with the discussion of your evidence through the same presentation. And if we can please have page 17 -- sorry, page 18, which is slide 17 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have no transcript on the screen. If perhaps ... the usher can assist me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you'd like that have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I will. I have it now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I think there's no problem in having the witness have the transcript before her. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, we see table 22 which is at page 29 of your report, and this table illustrates the integrated causes of death for each individual case. Now, can you first explain what "integrated" mean in this case, integrated causes of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with several sources reporting on their causes of death of the victims. The most important source were the reports produced by John Clark and two other pathologists with whom he worked on the issue. His reports on causes of death covered the victims that were exhumed in the fall of 2013 from Tomasica mine but didn't include the victims from earlier exhumations in Tomasica in 2004 and 2006. And also, his reports didn't include causes of death for the Jakarina Kosa victims. So in addition to Clark's reports, I also studied the documents, causes of death documents for the victims of 2004 and 2006 excavations in Tomasica and those from Jakarina Kosa. These were mainly autopsy reports that were available as part of the documents here of the collections of the Office of the Prosecutor. The "integrated," in this context, means that all these sources have been combined, as many documents as possible reporting on the causes were included in the integration, and only for 14 cases no cause of death reports were found. All other victims were covered. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this table presents the results of all of these sources integrated; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the result of the integration. Even though many documents were available, there is a considerable number of cases - 86 - for which cause of death remains unascertained or just not reported in the documents. The main reason for this is the fact that a large number of victims were moved from Tomasica to Jakarina Kosa and bodies were extremely fragmented and mixed, so many identifications were issued based on body part analysis, and in such cases cause of death could not be determined. Other than that, the picture that is presented in Table 22 is very similar to the results that Clark produced in his report and it is rightly so as the main source for the majority of cases I studied is his report on post-mortem investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, did you also consult the autopsy reports compiled by the Bosnian pathologist who worked with Mr. Clark on the -- after the post-mortem examinations of the human remains exhumed in Tomasica, 2013 I mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had at my disposal all of the documents, proof of death documents as we called them generally, provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the State Prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These documents included autopsies, DNA match reports, documents determining the identity of individuals, a number of investigative reports. In total, there were about 600 such documents. I paralleled my analysis based on Clark's data, other sources. I systematically consulted the proof of death documents from the Bosnian state prosecutor's office. I -- in particular, autopsies were important in the context of cause of death analysis. We received, as far as I remember, about 97 autopsies until the present time, which is not all but a considerable portion of the autopsies, and I compared these autopsies, cross-referenced them with the causes of death from my analysis and Clark's analysis. There is a table in my report, I think, 21, or - sorry, I have to check this - which reports on the result of this comparison --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And Dr. Tabeau, while you're double-checking the correct reference, I understand that Annex 3 is the place where we would find the list of all of these documents, and it's simply giving a reference -- is simply presenting the reference sources for the causes of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, the recently -- resubmitted, reorganised annex 3, which lists all the documents according to alphabetical list of victims' names, so it is easy searchable and all the documents available are listed next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record Dr. Tabeau is referring to reorganised version of Annex 3 that we have that she has produced according to an alphabetical record and that we have disclosed to the Defence, but that will not be part of her annexes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I have now the reference, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is table 20, page 28 of the English version of the report, which is the comparison of causes of death as Clark reported them and other sources I used versus the causes of death from the autopsies provided by the BH prosecutor office.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Dr. Tabeau, with regard to your annexes, I understand that part B of Annex 1 to your report is the place where you present the information on causes of death linked to each of the identified individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Annex 1 is the major annex. It has two parts. Part 1 is disappearance and identification information. And the second part, you called it Part B, gives cause of death, the integrated causes of death from my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm summarising the content of that part of the annex for the Chamber and for the record, because we won't have time to go into all of the annexes, and therefore I just wanted to say that that part lists alphabetically the names of each of the identified individual and provides for each of them the information related to the integrated causes of death, and you confirm that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to the next slide. Slide 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you also compared the list of identified victims from Tomasica with the victim list in the Mr. Mladic indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And your results are here presented in Table 42, which we find at page 43 of your report. And this table is now on the slide. Can you please briefly illustrate your results that are summarised in Table 42.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table has a simple structure. It reports on the 123 victims that were confirmed, that I was able to confirm in the so-called POD annex, which is basically a list of victims from the Scheduled Incidents in the fourth indictment, Mladic indictment. These victims are tabulated, shown here, according to the Scheduled Incident. Much of this table comes from the indictment. It is the incident, for example, A6.1, then the scope of the incident, then the municipality, concrete locality of the incident, date of the incidents, and in the very last column there is the number 3 for the A6.1, which means that three victims from the Tomasica mine were found among the victims of A6.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And so we see that the two Scheduled Incidents with the highest numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can we have the B/C/S zoomed in so that my client can actually read it? It's a little bit tiny on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I was asking whether -- so we see from the table that the two highest incidents -- the two incidents with the highest number of Tomasica identified victims are A6.6 and B13.1; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go on, Madam D'Ascoli, Mr. Ivetic has requested that the B/C/S either be zoomed in for his client to see. I don't see it being zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was, but I'm afraid that the problem lies in the layout of the B/C/S version, where a lot of room is reserved for spaces. Whereas, in the English version, the columns have been narrowed according with the text found in it. If there are any specific portions, Mr. Ivetic, you or Mr. Mladic would like to have a closer look at, don't hesitate to ask it to be zoomed in. Meanwhile, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, maybe if now after having zoomed on the left-hand side of the table we can do the same with the right-hand side so that both sides of the table in B/C/S can be better visible. That would probably solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, can you see it but you can't relate it any further. That, of course, is the problem. But if there would be a major problem, and we'll find out from Mr. Ivetic, then even a print-out could be made for those purposes. Meanwhile, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which columns are necessary at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I was basically commenting on the number of victims, which is the last column on the right-hand side of the table. But this should be read in conjunction with the very first one which indicates the incident for which we see the highest number of people. So unfortunately we will have to move from left to right and zoom in in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe, Dr. Tabeau, you can tell us what -- about the two incidents with the highest number of victims, Tomasica-identified victims, so that Mr. Mladic will hear your words and your explanation rather than having to look at the table. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to note that this table is also available from the report, B/C/S translation, it is Table 42. So if the report is available, it can also be seen there. The two incidents that are shown to have the highest numbers of victims is A6.6. These are killings of a number of men in several places, in Biscani predominantly, and in a number of hamlets; for example, Hegici, Mrkalji, Ravine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should refrain from seeking in any way to communicate with the public gallery and is advised to turn his face to -- to whomever. It's here where it happens, Mr. Mladic, not anywhere else. So if would you turn to the Chamber, to the witness, that would be appreciated, and the Chamber will not allow any communication with the public gallery. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The incident, A6.6, refers to killing men in several places - Biscani, hamlets of Hegici, Mrkalji, Ravine, Duratovici, Kalici, Lagici, and Cemernica - on or about 20th of July, 1992. There were 75 victims that I was able to confirm on the list of victims from this particular incident. The incident B13.1 relates to killing of approximately 150 people in room 3 at Keraterm camp on or about 24th and 25th of July, 1992. There were 28 victims confirmed as falling under this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Tabeau, I understand it is Annex 4 to your report, which lists alphabetically these 123 individuals providing for each of them information regarding their date of birth, place and date of disappearance, and the Scheduled Incidents of the Mladic indictment in which their names appear; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And again, I've summarised that because we won't have time to go into all of the details of your annexes and, in particular, Annex 4. Now, Dr. Tabeau, I want to move to some examples from your annexes, only part A of Annex 1, and then we will be returning to the remaining four slides of your presentation after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So if I can please have now on the screens 65 ter 31098. Actually, this is marked for identification with number P7451. And I would ask that this not to be broadcasted, please. If we can please go to page 10 of the English and 11 of the B/C/S. Dr. Tabeau, while this is coming up, the names of the victims in this document should not be stated aloud in open session as the document is not being displayed to the public.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And before we look at some examples, could you please briefly explain the information that we can find in Part A of Annex 1. Briefly because I will then ask you to move to walk us through the heading of the annex with concrete examples, so just to summarise what it is that we find in this part A of Annex 1.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of Tomasica victims. For every victim date of birth is reported, disappearance information of the victim - that is, place and date of disappearance - and then there are items like protocol number, case ID, ICMP ID, site name, site co-ordinates, et cetera. These are writings coming from the ICMP DNA match notifications that inform about the identification details of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And so let's move to a specific example. And if we can -- if can you focus on number 162 on this page, and I have to remind you again not to mention the name or place of disappearance of this individual while commenting about this case. 162.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can zoom in to start with the left-hand side of the table, zooming on number 162.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, first of all, Dr. Tabeau, the ID. So this is number 162, but we see --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- that the numbers in this column, the numbers before and after are not in a successive numeric order. So can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reference number, victim number, is the number associated with each victim as reported in the ICMP list from June 2014, the list of identifications. It was a list that reported jointly on the main cases and reassociations. The Annex 1 exclusively reports on the main cases. Reassociations have been separated, taken out from the list. This is because the whole report I made focuses on individuals, on persons, and not on DNA match reports available in total. So therefore, we see that the first victim has the number 152, next one 154. So 153 obviously is gone because it was a reassociation, an associated match report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And we do find the reassociation cases in annex 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, the column case names. Of course, these are -- this indicates the victim names, and I take it the name in bracket is the father's names of the identified individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, okay, date of birth is self-explanatory. Where did you take the date of birth information from?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of birth is reported after the ICMP, so it's the original data sent to us by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, we see, and I'm looking at number 162, that this individual was 65 years old when he meant missing; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Then -- okay. The column related to date and place of disappearance are ICRC-based. Is what the ICRC acronym was in the bracket in the heading of the column indicates; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your two hours will be over shortly before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And I'd ask if I could be ten minutes over just to introduce the new material. I had asked this relief last Thursday and I would be still within the nine hours that we asked, actually well below the limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would try to finish before the break and perhaps we would make -- take the break five minutes later that -- yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is agreeable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We can move out of this document and back into the -- Dr. Tabeau, I will continue now with your presentation but first I want to introduce the new material.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

There were a considerable of reassociations. I also determined more than 500, but jointly, main cases, and reassociations represented, as I said, 318 different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you recently analyse ICMP material related to the human remains exhumed from the Jakarina Kosa grave-site?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: Yes, this is a sample of cases from Jakarina Kosa. This sample represents cases that do not overlap with Tomasica cases. There were 211 such individuals as I determined, and this spreadsheet contains information about 211 non-Tomasica victims from Jakarina Kosa --

utterances.text: Can we now --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the document on Jakarina Kosa victims I produced recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this gives information on -- this provides basic statistics on the Jakarina Kosa identified individuals, according to the same methodology you used for your Tomasica report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. The two first tables --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, we will discussing that with the presentation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I will just ask that these three documents be marked for identification pending cross-examination.

utterances.text: That will be P7454, under seal, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.text: Marked for identification, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Then 65 ter 32738. This doesn't need to be under seal, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P7455, MFI, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli told us that there is no need to have it under seal. P7455 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And finally, 65 ter 32739. This should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P7456, MFI, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification, under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can I please have P7453, marked for identification, on the screens. And if we can move directly to slide 19 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I will be now just discussing briefly with you the last three slides of your presentation that summarise your analysis on the Jakarina Kosa identified individuals. While the document is coming up on the screen, did you follow the same methodology and uses the same sources as you earlier explained to the Court for this Jakarina Kosa analysis? And I just need a brief answer, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same methodology, the same sources, except for ICMP records that I downloaded myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. We now have slide 19 on the screens and this refers -- when it says page 1 Jakarina Kosa basic statistics, this refers to the document that has just been marked for identification with number P7455. This is your document, your summary of the basic statistic on Jakarina Kosa; correct? It is take from there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you briefly summarise the findings that we see in this table.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First table summarizes the overall numbers of victims for Jakarina Kosa. The number I mentioned earlier today, 318, is the number in the last row of this table. It is a sum of two numbers from the table. The first one in the first row, which is 310, and that is the overall number of named Jakarina Kosa victims. That's represented by the main cases. This number, therefore, represents unique different individuals; and the second number is in the second-last row, which is 8. And this is the overall number of not-yet named but unique DNA profiles. The so-called uniques that should be taken together with the first one. So the overall total is 318 different individuals buried in Jakarina Kosa. Of these individuals, 99 are overlapping with Tomasica. In my report, it is 98. I worked with an update of ICMP data from June 2014 to obtain the 98. Now I used a one-year-later data of the ICMP and confirmed instead of 98, 99 cases split between Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now of the 211 identified individuals that were solely exhumed from Jakarina Kosa not connected to Tomasica cases, you calculated how many of these individuals appear in the proof of death annex that was previously introduced during your testimony in November 2013. And for the record, this is P2797. I see that this number is 61 in the lower table; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. It is 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the breakdown of this information, I will go to the -- I will ask to go to the next slide, number 20. And, Dr. Tabeau, if you're looking specifically at the 61 Jakarina Kosa victims that appeared in the earlier proof of death annex, P2797, can you tell us briefly which incidents are these victims mainly linked to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are five incidents, among them the two ones I already discussed previously. It is A6.6 and B13.1. But starting from the first row of this table, we see victims under incident A6.1, the second one is A6.4, then A6.6, B13.1, and the last B13.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I'm following correctly these are persons not related to Tomasica for which information was already available in November of 2013 when the witness testified. And now for the first time we're hearing them linking the bodies to indictment charges. I respectfully submit again that the Prosecutor is going outwith the scope of the reopening and is attempting to rehabilitate their case in the midst of the Defence case after having rested the same. And I would want that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any response, Ms. D'Ascoli?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. These victims were already identified in the proof of death annex, and the information on them -- and the information that was available at the time, it is already on the record. Ms. Tabeau has added the -- the linkage with the -- with the exhumed cases, and -- well, sorry. I'm saying that this linkage was already there, so it's just now part of an analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Link --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- between the exhumation place being Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think what Mr. Ivetic argues is that you are adding now something for victims - that is, you linked them to the incident - whereas, first of all, this is not directly related to Tomasica because these were persons whose remains were found exclusively in Jakarina Kosa. And second, that you're now adding something by linking those of which you say we knew about them already to specific incidents in the fourth indictment. That's the issue. Could you please respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This information was provided and we asked Dr. Tabeau to produce this information in response to the Defence challenges during the reopening to the figures for the bodies exhumed from -- from Jakarina Kosa, and I'm prepared to detail these challenges, if that would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you said you'd like to have it on the record. Would you like to have a ruling on it? Not that the Chamber is going to give it right away but that at least we'll consider whether this stays within the limits as outlined in our reopening decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We're on the same page. I assumed you would need some time on this, but I do want a ruling. I do consider my statement as an objection to this evidence being led during this reopening.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will not stop at this moment Ms. D'Ascoli right away, but we'll consider whether this Chamber will take into account the evidence as presented now in view of your objections, but we prefer to carefully analyse again exactly what we're looking at and where the limits are in view of our reopening decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I continue. Just to stress that the direct link between the two sides was mentioned, expressed in paragraph 30 of our motion to reopen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, that's one of the things we'll consider when analysing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I will then continue and move to the final slides which provides the overall number of identified individual across the two sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Dr. Tabeau, I will briefly ask you to comment on slide 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This slide has a statement that victims from Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa belong together, and further there is a little table that shows the number of victims from Tomasica, 385. Further, Jakarina Kosa victims not in Tomasica lists 211, that is the cases I just discussed. Further, there is 8 cases, the so-called uniques from Jakarina Kosa which gives, together, an overall total of victims in Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa, 604. This table and this overall total, the statement on this slide have the reasons in several findings that I have made for Jakarina Kosa victims. Among the 211 victims, 103 had exactly the same places of disappearance and dates of disappearance as Tomasica victims. It's a very considerable portion of them, number of them, having the same disappearance details. Further, I analysed their ethnic composition. I analysed sex distribution, age distribution, places of disappearance, their residence in 1991, and I saw the same or highly similar results as the ones for victims exhumed from Tomasica. So that the foundation for me making these statements on this slight.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And we do find the details of all of this information that you just discussed in your document on the basic statistics from Jakarina Kosa; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And the document is now marked for identification with P7455. Thank you, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, the issue between the parties at this moment is whether they belong together because of the similarities in the population or whether they do not belong together because the bodies were found in and the bodily remains were found in Jakarina Kosa only and not in Tomasica. That apparently is the issue which we'll have to consider. Ms. Tabeau, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's been sometime since our last meeting in cross-examination, so I wish to remind you again to focus precisely on my questions so that we may efficiently move as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to have just a few questions about your CV, so if we can call up P7448 [Realtime transcript read in error "P7488"]. Perhaps while we wait for that, I'm sure it will come to no surprise to you that your CV shows that since the last time you were in court with us you're again employed directly by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal since March of 2014. My question is this in a full-time or part-time capacity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a full-time capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. You called P7448.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is given here as "7488."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, you didn't misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, madam, in terms of your full-time employment with the Office of the Prosecutor, what type of contract is it in terms of the level and the number of years?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same level contract as I had previously, and my contract ends by December 31st of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And since March of 2014, has all your work at the Office of the Prosecutor been solely related to studying the evidence as to the Tomasica mass grave and the Jakarina Kosa bodies related to Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not solely. I have been performing research into victimisation in the Mladic case but also working on other things. It is simply the same type of responsibilities as I used to have in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have an approximation as the percentage of your time spent on Tomasica or perhaps in terms of number of total hours that you've spent on the demographic evidence relating to Tomasica since March of 2014?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was that I was spending a considerable amounts of time after I came in March until, say, end of June 2014, because it was the time when the evidence was collected and pieces were sent from Bosnia to the Office of the Prosecutor now and then, and it was still a matter of integrating the pieces, updating the lists I was making. So redoing these things all over and over again. But once I finished the report, I simply stopped working on Tomasica, and it was only recently that I started again analysing things, re-reading the report, looking at Jakarina Kosa records, so it is not that I was working all the time since March 2014 on Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, did you perform any work relating to Tomasica before March 2014 when you returned to full-time employment at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was employed first time - that is, between the year 2000 and 2011 - I had short episodes of work on the victims reported missing from Prijedor and more broadly Autonomous Region of Krajina. I made, I think, two reports on that in -- around the year of 2002, 2003, I believe. But not that I completed projects exclusively on Tomasica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this time around in your written report I did not see any credits for any co-authors. Did you, in fact, work alone on this report related to Tomasica or did you have any assistants?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked alone on this report and didn't any assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to follow any of the media coverage as to Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not following systematically media reports, because I had, in the past, opportunities to see much bias in these reports. So it is not a source from which I learn and which I take it and use in my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn to your report, which I believe is P7449, relating to Tomasica. And if we could turn to the -- for now, page 1 in both languages. And this is the contents of your report. Doctor, last time you were here we talked about over 70 criteria, or you called them I think keys, which you used when matching names with the various databases. This report on Tomasica that is before us does not seem to identify how many keys were used in the Tomasica report, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not so that I provide with every report an overview of matching criteria I have used for matching various lists with each other. So this particular report does not contain such a list. The list you have mentioned was made available as part of the 2009 integrated Srebrenica report, provided as example an explanation of how the matching is done. I still stand by this list and by the criteria. But in every project I use some of these criteria as they are in this table and some additional criteria formulated in line with the logic of that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's entirely what I expected, Doctor, and that's why I asked you to precisely tell us how many matching criteria or keys were used for the Tomasica report and what precisely those keys were.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to be more specific about your question. If you say matching of the Tomasica list, then have you to tell me with what source, and then I can explain more specifically what was the criteria based about. Still, I will not give you the concrete criteria because I don't have them at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do the concrete criteria exist somewhere in your office?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean in a form of the list, like the list of 70, then my answer is no, they don't. Other than that, I can provide you with the logic of my matching for any two sources that you will mentioned [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, you've provided us with a report listing multiple sources, and you've provided us your opinions of matches obtained, and I'm interested in finding out what methodology that you utilised. Would you agree with me that knowing what keys were used is essential to understanding your methodology?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, isn't it true that the witness offers to explain what keys she used in any match she established, so therefore the information is offered to you. It's just a matter of asking the right question. Ms. Tabeau, if I understand your testimony well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then let re-ask the question that I started with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely how many matching criteria were used for each of the sources and what precisely those keys were for each of the sources that you analysed for purposes of the Tomasica report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau earlier said that you have to specify which match you had in mind and that she can then, if I understand her well, reconstruct exactly what criteria she used, what key she used in that specific match. So if you would to begin with start with one of the matches, then we could see whether it works or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me do it this way then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, would you be in a position to prepare and provide a listing based upon your recollection of what keys you use in matching the various names with the varies databases for all of the matches that are contained in the Tomasica report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the matches, it is indeed a lot of work, but I certainly am willing to -- to accommodate your request. It will be a lot of additional work for me, so reconstructing the matching process and listing the criteria will take time, so if I am to do that, then I -- please must be offered some additional time do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I definitely did not intend for you to do it in the courtroom. My question is, though, isn't it correct that a list of keys is generally in your field created before one provides the work of checking to match and that therefore there should be a list of keys that were tried - not necessarily find a match on each key, but all the lists that were in your universe that you were examining; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say that I thought you answered this yes question earlier, that it's not necessarily so in every case that you have a list of matching.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said. Now, if I would be to provide the list of criteria, I have to go through the matching process again and reconstruct the criteria. But I think that Mr. Ivetic sees the process of matching in a very formal way in the sense that one starts with a formal list of criteria and then goes through the entire list to end with a result at the end. As a matter of fact, a very long list of criteria, say 70, might be finished after five first steps because the records simply match very well and then there is no need even to go through the rest of the list. So the matching process is basically cross-referencing of two related lists or two lists expected to be related to each other, and mainly by comparison of the names on the two lists and dates of birth, other information on the lists, one draws conclusions about the similarity of potentially related cases. If there is an identity of reporting on the two lists of a given person, then a match can be easily declared. If there are slight differences in the spelling of names or in the dates of birth, then one has to decide whether the differences are acceptable and a match can be declared or a match cannot be declared. In some cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I think you've gone beyond the question that I asked you, and I'd like to ask a follow-up. Would you agree with me by not including the number nor type of keys that you relied upon for purposes of your matching in the report, it makes it rather difficult for another specialist in your field to assess and opine as to the accuracy of your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute. Before we continue, although I think that the record is not precise, that the last intervention by the Bench was done by Judge Moloto, and I understood his remark as seeking verification of one of the previous answers as given by Ms. Tabeau, and therefore I considered her to respond to that implicit request for verification of a good understanding of the testimony. And, Mr. Ivetic, I think it was not up to you at that moment to stop the witness and to say that she went beyond your question because she was responding to an intervention by Judge Moloto. If you would like to finish that, Ms. Tabeau, you may resume from where you said: "In some cases," where Mr. Ivetic intervened. And then after that, Mr. Ivetic, I take it that Ms. Tabeau will further consider whether she has answered your question or that you'll further consider whether she has answered your question put to her before the intervention of Judge Moloto. Ms. Tabeau, if you'd like to resume, if there's anything to be added, then you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to add that in a small number of cases, no match is possible through an automated procedure, and then what I do in the end I just search manually for certain names of victims in related sources. I do it one by one. I do it because certain sources contain deformations of names, like there are no spaces between first name and father's name and family name, so there is no way I can find a person through an automated procedure. I have to do it differently on an individual basis. So, in the end my matching might be limited to searching for records of a small group of individuals which brings me some results, but some are just not reported and remain unmatched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could ask one additional question. If you have several keys, I do understand that logic requires that you seek for positive -- the keys positively matching?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's one. And you said, if I have some, then it would already allow for a conclusion. But I do understand also that part of the matching process could be to exclude that there are any contradictions. Now, you've told us about -- that after some of these corresponding facts that you could draw a conclusion that there's a match. Let's just -- just for my understanding, let's assume the date of birth is the same, the name of the person is the same, the name of the father is the same, the place where they lived is the same. Now, that all strongly suggests that we're talking about the same persons. At the same time, if the DNA, for example, does not match, then there must be perhaps a very unlikely explanation or there must be a mistake somewhere in the system. Could you tell us something about the remaining keys perhaps falsifying what you thought to be a positive match on the basis of those other keys.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is correct that I basically concentrate on comparing the personal information about the victims, that would be the names - first, father's, family - and the date of birth and the place of residence in cases of which I want to learn more. If this is identical or largely the same in two sources, then I declare a match. DNA is only reported in one source. This is the ICMP list of identifications. The matching of the persons listed by the ICMP is still based on the comparison of personal information of victims; but, of course, when making matching for the victims from Prijedor, I wouldn't go and look for a match in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina because these people were living in Prijedor, in this area, so there must be a consistency of the personal information but also the residence. So it has to come together consistently. Must corroborate each other, you know, each piece of information. And once a match is declared, then there is the DNA report and a site report, you know, where the person was exhumed from, et cetera, et cetera. So no matching is done starting from the DNA and the site information without a list because that's not possible simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's not linked to any identified person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps the DNA was a bad example. Are there any other keys that could finally contradict and then, let's forget about the DNA, but if you have persons with the same name, same date of birth, same place of living, then of course that's still not for the full 100 per cent makes them the same persons, and there's still a possibility, although perhaps statistically a very small possibility, that these are not the same persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is why I do the matching with the entire census, 1991 population census, to see how many individuals with exact same names and very similar dates of birth are reported there and from which areas, from which parts of Bosnia. So just to exclude the false positives of which I know they couldn't be falling under the project I am working on. So it is called blocking. There is a formal procedure in matching in theory and practice, that by excluding the false positives and focusing on blocks of related information one can assure high quality of the matching process results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we're talking in terms of probability of 99.99 per cent or is that the kind of -- the basis for your conclusions, but perhaps I'm entering the area of statistics where I should --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't go for giving Your Honours a formal probability as the ICMP does in the case of their matching process. I don't think I can provide such a number, especially that the lists that I have been matching represent different situations. They have now different numbers of records, so I don't think I would be then able to calculate probability straight away, say. It would be a challenge to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. At the same time, of course, if you say it could be -- fall below 80 per cent, then, of course, it might be of some concern to us. If it falls below -- what region approximately are we working in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the matching rate with the census for the Tomasica list was 92 per cent, which is not below 80 per cent. I think it is a high per cent. And it is not 99.9999, as we have in the ICMP matching procedures, but it is very well above 90 per cent. It is 92 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I -- both my colleague and I interrupted you in your last question. I don't know whether you're satisfied with the answer yet or whether you'd seek further explanations from the witness, so I give it in your hands again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to ask you again: Would you agree that by not including the number nor type of keys used in your matching it makes it very difficult for your report to be checked by another specialist in your area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can move on and look at page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S. In the B/C/S, it will be the second paragraph from the bottom; and in the English, it's the second paragraph up from the subheading 2.6, and here you say, Doctor: "Cause of death information by Dr. Clark has been invaluable in producing proof of death for Tomasica victims." Doctor, would you have to defer to Dr. Clark as to cause of death, or do you think there is some other source more reliable than Dr. Clark as to cause of death for these persons found in Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what I said in the report, that Clark's information about causes of death is invaluable, I still stand by this statement. I also used other sources for cause of deaths as you know, because I mentioned this today. Jakarina Kosa autopsies. I also used some autopsies from 2004 and 2006 excavations in Tomasica. But, me, as a demographer and statisticians, I'm not the person to determine the cause of death, so it has to be in the hands of other specialists, pathologists; in this case, as Dr. Clark himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you feel that you have been fair and impartial in the preparation of your report including the use of Dr. Clark's expert opinions about cause of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, my role was to take the existing sources of information, also about causes of death, and integrate this information with the victim records of the Tomasica victims, which I did. I did read the report of Dr. Clark, of course. I had gone through his annexes and I find this material very useful, and I included it as very relevant to the analysis of causes of death. I think that I was impartial because, as I am saying, this is not me who determined the causes. I am just presenting the causes. And in the end, I believe it is the autopsies in which pathologists will take another look at related causes of death and draw conclusions about the causes of death of individuals, is the ultimate source, I think, to look at. Yet, there is a table in my report in which I compared the autopsies for about 60-something individuals. I compared the reports from the autopsies by pathologists with the information as I integrated it from the sources that I had at my disposal, and I found no major or even very many discrepancies. It is all highly consistent, the two perspectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to call up 1D5782, and I'll be looking for page 78 of that document. This will be the transcript from Dr. Clark's testimony in this courtroom last week. Again, page 78, which should correlate to page 36651 of the transcript, and I would like to focus on lines 10 through 14, which you can read and I'll read into the record. It starts off: "Q. I would like to put one last question regarding this topic by way of a conclusion. "Is it correct that, as a scientist, you cannot exclude the possibility that any or some of the people were killed in combat? "A. Yes, I can't -- I can't exclude that." Is this finding by Dr. Clark highly consistent with your results in doing your work as to the bodies recovered from Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't any -- I didn't study any sources based on which I could say that someone died in combat or in non-combat situation. I actually draw no conclusions about that. So whatever Mr. Clark said in his testimony, it is his opinion, but I cannot make any statements at this moment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, madam, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I think it would be fair to this witness to tell her that Dr. Clark took, as a matter of fact, the same position. That he wouldn't know whether people died in combat and for that he couldn't exclude that. I do understand your answer to be in this respect the same, that your research was not focused on whether people died in combat or not and that therefore you can't exclude anything because you haven't studied it. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There is not any foundation for me to exclude or include or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And that was, as a matter of fact, Mr. Ivetic, was the gist of the evidence given by Dr. Clark as well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you then renouncing your conclusion on page 47 of your report that says: "All in all, a significant evidence was presented in this report which supports the conclusion that all Tomasica victims died violent deaths in extremely dramatic circumstances of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing in the Prijedor municipality and as part of the ARK ethnic cleansing campaign."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this statement, first of all, has to do with the fact that Tomasica victims were all buried in an unmarked mine, that many bodies were removed to another site, bodies were fragmented so dramatically that even I could see the circumstances of how this process was looking like at some point. So the signs of injuries in their bodies as reported by Clark but also by other sources, Jakarina Kosa autopsies, other autopsies, 2004/2006 autopsies, all this leaves no doubt that these were violent deaths. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But how do you differentiate between violent deaths in combat and the violent deaths in ethnic cleansing, the word you used in your report, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic cleansing is supported by other findings in my report. I'm referring to the part of the report that shows the results of the analysis of missing persons from the Prijedor municipality and Tomasica victims in this context, and also missing persons from the ARK. There are very clear findings there showing that non-Serbs were targeted, especially the Muslims who disappeared in very large numbers in -- contradictory to other ethnic groups, that men actually disappeared in the first place in large numbers, and men at military age, say, between, say, 18 and 65 or something like that. So it is a picture that is actually quite indicative of an ethnic cleansing process, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, having just testified under oath that did you not consider and therefore cannot exclude combat, how can you then exclude combat as a means of death that would be different than ethnic cleansing, the word you used in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't exclude combat. I didn't draw any conclusions about the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then do you feel that your conclusions as to ethnic cleansing are complete since you did not take into account the potential impact or role of combat as to the bodies recovered from Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the report I made is not about the ethnic cleansing in the first place. It is about the victims from Tomasica in the first place --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I beg to differ. The conclusion I just read is the penultimate conclusion of your report. I put it to you that it is the basis of your report and it is the key part of your report. If you do not want us to rely upon that conclusion, please say so.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to me I see a clear picture of ethnic cleansing based on the records I studied, based on the records of missing persons, from the Prijedor municipality - in particular from the Prijedor municipality and from the ARK area as such. The fact that that many victims went missing on a few days in July, the 20th, 23, 4th, and 5th, these are huge numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, Doctor, are you then taking back what you said a few moments ago, that ethnic cleansing is not the subject of your report?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered this question several times -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think she has at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Ivetic, I would appreciate if you do not interrupt each other. I leave it to the witness whether she thinks that she has answered the question and whether she has been given sufficient opportunity to explain her answer. The question was, Ms. Tabeau, whether you're taking back what you said a few moments ago, that ethnic cleansing was not the subject of your report. Do you think that you have sufficiently answered that question or would you like to add anything to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I discuss the ethnic cleansing in my report as the context for the Tomasica victims. It is unavoidable to mention the words "ethnic cleansing" as in my view the deaths, the killings of the Tomasica victims were part of the ethnic cleansing. And, of course, there is some results, quite some results in my report that support ethnic cleansing considerably. I am speaking of ethnic cleansing from my own experience. It is not the first time that I have been working on the 92 victims, Tomasica victims, also victims from the ARK and Prijedor municipality. I studied other sources of information and made other reports. From my experience and from the work I have done in the past as well, there is quite some support in this report in this work for the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I'm really confused. Because you say now in my view the death, the killing of the Tomasica victims were part of the ethnic cleansing. Other hand, Dr. Clark says at transcript page 36684 that he cannot even exclude the possibility that all persons exhumed from Tomasica were the result of combat, and yet you have told us you did not consider combat. You did not look at combat. You did not exclude combat. So how can you sit here today and say to a degree of scientific certainty that all the deaths are related to ethnic cleansing having not even considered combat which Dr. Clark, your main source, who you said is invaluable for cause of death, said that he can't exclude? Explain that for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Ivetic says, I'll take the transcript, you're now saying that all persons exhumed from Tomasica were the result of combat -- no, were the result of ethnic cleansing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I remember what he said but I don't see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will certainly be willing to give us exactly the --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- page and line reference where the witness would have said --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line 19, page 49. The witness's own words.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness own words, reading the whole sentence, is: "It is unavoidable to mention the words 'ethnic cleansing' as in my view the deaths, the killings of the Tomasica victims were part of the ethnic cleansing." This is not accurately characterised by Mr. Ivetic when he then turns to say that Ms. Tabeau said that all of the victims of the Tomasica exhumed victims were victims of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you please rephrase your question and when referring to what the witness said be -- to quote her literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just add before Mr. Ivetic talks, I think where Mr. Ivetic refers to all persons he is talking about Dr. Clark, not Madam Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And that was at transcript page 73 -- 36684. But let's see if can I clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: But that again is not a conclusion. Dr. Clark just said he could not exclude, but it is not presented in the form of a certainty or the conclusion that the witness made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's clear, that Dr. Clark, in this respect, did not draw any conclusions because he had not studied the matter, and therefore he could not exclude that 1 per cent or 100 per cent of the victims had died in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's the crux of my question to Dr. Tabeau. How can she conclude that they were the result of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, they --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: She did not exclude that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, they -- we should clearly distinguish between whether we are talking about all of the victims as referred to in at least the later questions to Dr. Clark, or to any other group or number of persons. Would you please rephrase your question clearly and with great precision Mr. Ivetic, and then we'll hear the answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you believe that all the bodies exhumed from Tomasica were the result of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can only tell what kind of causes of death were reported for them on sources like Clark's report and other documents related to the causes of death. I didn't study any events like combat or other events that led to their deaths. What I tried to do is I tried to define where and when the events were taking place, and in order to learn more about these events, you would need additional sources and additional expertise. Yet at the same time from the analysis, my demographic analysis of disappearance data, I still stand by the conclusion that there was ethnic cleansing in these territories at that time. Yet, again, I cannot tell how every single victim died, whether it was a part of the ethnic cleansing campaign or any other event. I can tell you that these were the facts: There was ethnic cleansing, because it is clear from the disappearance information of the victims buried in Tomasica, buried in Jakarina Kosa, the victims who disappeared from Prijedor, the victims who disappeared from ARK. This is a very strong indication of the ethnic cleansing in these territories at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If may just ask one more question before the break. You mentioned, let me quote you precisely, that you "can only tell what kind of causes of death were reported for them on sources like Clark's report and other documents related to the causes of death." Madam, will you agree with me that neither Dr. Clark's report nor the other autopsy reports listed ethnic cleansing as a cause of death for any of the Tomasica exhumed bodies. That is a word you inserted into the analysis; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing is that Dr. Clark didn't report ethnic cleansing but he did report short distance gun-shots, execution style gun-shots in the heads, back of the heads, et cetera, et cetera. So that confirms my conclusion, as well as his conclusion, that these deaths were violent. Whether the events were part of the ethnic cleansing campaign, yes, I think they were, because that is what I see from the disappearance information of the victims. This is supportive and indicative, highly indicative of an ethnic cleansing campaign in these territories in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But further neither Dr. Clark nor me could tell you more about the events themselves.
