utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I respectfully ask you to answer my question. Did Dr. Clark or the other autopsies you look at use the word "ethnic cleansing" as cause of death or is that something you yourself inserted into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The thing is that Dr. Clark didn't report ethnic cleansing but -- and then the witness started explaining that she used data among those Dr. Clark reports as to the causes of death but also other information which led her to conclude that the information she received both from Dr. Clark and from other sources fit into what the witness understands to be ethnic cleansing -- an ethnic cleansing campaign. So the witness has answered in the beginning the question, but if you would like to put any follow-up question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one more before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more before the break. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, you mentioned violent deaths. Do you consider deaths in the course of combat to be violent or non-violent in nature, as you understand that word as you've used it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, I think if we speak of combat, well, these are violent deaths, of course, but of a different type than if people are killed not being combatants and not being engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll wait until after the break. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take the break first. But as we did before, the Chamber would prefer that Mr. Mladic is escorted out of the courtroom first. We -- then we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00. Mr. Mladic, you are to leave the courtroom first. No speaking aloud. Mr. Mladic, you should leave the courtroom first. You'll be escorted by security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you think differentiating between combat-related deaths and those from ethnic cleansing is irrelevant for purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said it is irrelevant for the purposes of my report, but I was just not able to study sources that would be telling me about the combat and non-combat incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Given that you concede combat is also a violent death, different than people killed as non-combatants or killed not in combat, will you agree that there exists a possibility that some or all Tomasica bodies may equally be from combat as they may be from what you've called ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude this option.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that where a pathologist lists cause of death as being unknown or unascertained, then you as a demographer do not have an actual cause of death for that individual?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no cause of death reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you give us any statistical data about what percentage of the Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa bodies had unascertained or unknown causes of death listed by the forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we just saw this table earlier today. This is Table 22, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that for both Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is for Tomasica victims. 22 is for Tomasica victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So could you then answer my question: What percentage of all the bodies from Jakarina Kosa and Tomasica would you say the autopsy reports listed unascertained or unknown causes of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For both of them jointly, I cannot. Also not for Jakarina Kosa, because I did not have all the reports for all the victims studied. I just looked for the reports for the victims overlapping between Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider individuals with an unascertainable cause of death, would they, in your opinion, be victims of ethnic cleansing as is listed in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I spoke about ethnic cleansing, I was having in mind the information about the disappearance of victims in combination with the information about the violent nature of their deaths. And, of course, for Jakarina Kosa, we don't have the information about causes of death for all the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So let's focus on the 22 victim, as you call them, I call them bodies, from Tomasica for which there were unascertained causes of death. Do you include those in your conclusion of Tomasica victims being the result of an ethnic cleansing campaign?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 22 is a wrong number, sir. There were many more victims from Tomasica with unascertained causes of death. In Table 22, it is 86 victims mentioned with unascertained cause of death. Whether they are part of the ethnic cleansing, well, sir, as I mentioned, what I concluded in my report is that all victims from Tomasica died of violent deaths, and it is disregarding whether the cause of death was well determined or unascertained. There is a very good reason for the fact that such a large number of causes of death remain unascertained, this reason is the moving of the bodies, a large number of the bodies, from Tomasica to Jakarina Kosa. So in many instances, individuals were identified through the DNA matching process on the basis of the analysis of a bone sample, a small part of the entire body, and in these cases causes of death could not be determined and remain unascertained. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is the reason that cause of death is unavailable. But there is evidence about splitting of the bodies. This is the analysis of reassociations that I presented in my report. And the mere fact of moving the bodies in large numbers from one site to another, and fragmented bodies, and a huge number of reassociations, tells about -- that these were not just victims buried in a regular cemetery with the names listed on -- on the -- on the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can summarise full circle, according to you the 86 bodies with unascertained causes of death from Tomasica would still be included in the group that you say on page 47 as all Tomasica victims who died violent deaths in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivetic, at page 56, from line 5, you asked the question: "Okay. Would you agree with me that where a pathologists lists cause of death as being unknown or unascertained, then you as a demographer do not have an actual cause of death for that individual?" The answer was: "Yes, there is no cause of death reported." Now you're asking the same question in a slightly different formulation. So obviously if she has -- she -- there's no cause of death, then she can't include them either as combat victims or as cleansing victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you. But I don't think that's what she just said. I think she is including them as being ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No -- but -- let's let her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's why I want to know the answer. Are these 86 persons persons for whom she has concluded that they were victims of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But isn't it logical from that prior answer that they couldn't be because they are, as she says, yes, there is no cause of death reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Dr. Tabeau confirms that for those 86 persons they couldn't be victims of ethnic cleansing, I'll move on, but I don't think she will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I confirm that I said in my report, and I would like to quote from my report, it is page 47, the last paragraph of the report: "All in all, a significant evidence was presented in this report which supports the conclusion that all Tomasica victims died violent deaths in extremely dramatic circumstances of a broader campaign of the ethnic cleansing in the Prijedor municipality and as part of the ARK ethnic cleansing campaign." So my statement here is about the violent nature of these deaths, and I'm saying all victims died violent deaths in dramatic circumstances. It is not only about causes of death. The conclusion about the dramatic circumstances is -- has its foundation in the fact how they were buried. It is not just a regular grave that they were buried in. It is an old mine, Tomasica, or Jakarina Kosa, where the bodies were dropped, and for whatever reason, but obviously a significant reason, at some point a large number of bodies were moved and split. The image of these split bodies is not nothing. It is a further continuation of the -- of the violent nature that already was there when the bodies were buried in an unmarked grave without their names listed and without even knowing by people that bodies are buried there. So I stand by this statement: All victims died violent deaths, disregarding the fact that for 86 of them the cause of death remains unascertained. And these 86 are body parts, fragments, legs, hands, pieces of bodies found separately in a different location than the rest of the body. That is the violent character of these deaths. So it has nothing to do with the ascertained causes of death as such. There are good reasons for this, that we don't have the causes of death, and I'm sure if we go to Jakarina Kosa, we will see even more unascertained causes of death for these victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Ms. Tabeau, the fact that the body or the body parts were found in graves which were of a massive nature rather than individual graves, not necessarily - at least theoretically - means that all of them died from violent causes. I mean, you couldn't exclude for the possibility that someone got a stroke when seeing, for example, that others were shot in the head and were sharing the same fate to end up in such a grave. Purely theoretically, perhaps, but I'm just exploring exactly where the demographic expertise allows for such -- such conclusions as you just expressed, that all of them died a violent death or whether, at least theoretically, there's still a possibility that they did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course this kind of a stroke is a possibility. I cannot exclude this kind of causes of death --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or combat is another one. I absolutely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still being a violent death but not in the context as you describe it here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But generally, as I see these victims, how they were buried and how many of them had -- were determined causes of death, which were all of violent nature - there were determined causes, we are talking about gun-shots of all kinds, doesn't seem these were gun-shots acquired in combat from the fact -- you know, I didn't write it. Clark wrote it that is fact. I rely on somebody's else opinion in that. But it seems that these were short distance, violent shots that killed these people. Of course, we have 86 cases. 86 individuals for whom there are no causes of deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore you could not exclude for any or even all of those that they would have died not from a violent cause, although you would consider it not very likely to have happened. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The gravamen of Mr. Ivetic's argument is not on violence. It's on the kind of violence that you describe. He says how do you distinguish between violence from ethnic cleansing and violence from combat? Now, he agrees with you that this was -- this may have been a violent death. He quarrels with ethnic cleansing. That's the gravamen of his argument, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand this as well. And from the analysis I made in my report and in previous reports and other studies, I see the evidence of ethnic cleansing. The way people were reported missing, who, the ethnicity, sex patterns, the huge displacement of the population of the same character. I had myself a report in this case in which I discuss the patterns in internal displacement and refugees, so all this is supportive of ethnic cleansing, and I see it as a demographer because I have evidence of it. I'm not a military analyst. I cannot correlate information about combat actions in the same area in the same period with the patterns I see in the disappearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think I understand why you come to that conclusion. I don't know whether Mr. Ivetic wants to carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another part of the report. If we can return to P7449 in e-court, and I believe, according to my notes, it will be page 6 in both languages. And in English, it's the last part of the first paragraph, and in B/C/S it will be the bottom of the page. And I now quote: "POD is -- is more a label than an actual data item. It indicates Prijedor for almost all victims but not specific places of disappearance within the Prijedor municipality." First of all, just to be clear, are you here talking about ICMP's records as to the Tomasica bodies?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so in your opinion, the place of disappearance data from ICMP is not reliable. Is that really what you are saying here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I want to stress that I am not in the position to assess the reliability of the ICMP reporting on the disappearance other than by comparing the places of disappearance reported by ICMP with the places reported by ICRC, for example, other sources, and Prijedor is just a general term that ICMP is using for all the individuals, all except I think for two or something, and it is used in the -- in the sense of the Prijedor municipality, which is very general as a report of disappearance, whereas ICRC and Prijedor Book of Missing are much more specific with regard to the places. So -- but they are not contradictory in the sense that all small villages that ICRC reports or Prijedor Book of Missing reports are within the Prijedor municipality. But going back to your question, whether I consider ICMP reporting of the disappearance information reliable, I think they just don't focus on this information. They have it because they collect it as part of the blood collection process, and then if we want to have it requested, "we" I mean the Office of the Prosecutor, they will provide it without having any value or reliability assessment attached. In Srebrenica cases, for example, all Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to ask about Srebrenica. We have that evidence. I'd like to stick to Tomasica, which is what we were told we were doing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness wants to explain by comparison other situations, she's allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So in Srebrenica cases, the ICMP allocated the term either as "the forest" or "Potocari" and no more places at all. It was either the forest or Potocari. And the date of disappearance for every victim, Srebrenica victim, was 11th of July. So it was more like a flagging of victims as related to Srebrenica than providing the actual information about the -- the concrete circumstances, that means dates and places of disappearance. And here the situation is quite similar for Tomasica victims. They used this label Prijedor for -- for the disappearance, place of disappearance. With the dates of disappearance, they are much more specific. So they come into dates and report the different dates of disappearance. But again, it is just as they have it at hand without any assessment procedure or corrections, improvement attempts. They just report it as available from the family members who donated blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you have, as such, no doubt about whether they disappeared in the Prijedor municipality and that that information, therefore, is -- you have no reason to think it's unreliable but it lacks precision which -- a precision which perhaps would allow for a further analysis which is impossible if we only know that they disappeared in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is very correct. I have one section in the report in which I actually compare the ICMP reporting with the ICRC reporting and the reporting by the Prijedor Book of Missing of both place and dates of disappearance, and the three are highly consistent except that Prijedor lacks the detail that I need for the analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be accepted practice in the field of demography to assign a grade or reliability factor to a particular source that is being used and to report the same in your demographic report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so could you please help me then why are you unable to provide such a grade or reliability factor for the data from ICMP, demographically speaking?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the simple reason that I don't rely on this source. When I discuss the disappearance information of the victims, I use mainly the ICRC records in combination with the records from the Book of Missing, Prijedor Book of Missing, and I am not using basically the ICMP disappearance information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you in a position to report a grade or reliability factor for these other sources that you did rely upon?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you want me to provide. If you want a number, a single number, then I don't have such a number. But I do have an opinion about the reliability of both ICRC and the Prijedor Book of Missing. I have been working with ICRC, in particular, for many years, and several times I studied the reliability of this list and assessed the list as very reliable, as a matter of fact, although not free of certain deficiencies like gaps in the data or incorrect dates of birth, for example, victims. These kind of issues are there, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us about the ICRC list. What about the other sources you use? Can you give us an assessment in demographic terms of the quality or reliability factor of the other sources you use for the Tomasica report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important source is, of course, the ICMP list of DNA match notifications, and I certainly have a very high opinion about the ICMP records, and this is a reliable list that I have no reasons to doubt. ICMP have been used -- again, many times I have used the ICMP lists many times in various cases. I unfortunately have to mention Srebrenica again, Mr. Ivetic, as it was the most substantial case in which these records were used, but also in other cases. I used the Prijedor Book of Missing which is a sources made locally in the Prijedor municipality. This source is less reliable than the ICRC list, yet it highly overlaps with the ICRC list; however, there are many more deficiencies in the Prijedor Book of Missing like missing pieces of information or errors in the date of birth. I studied also the 1991 census, which I assessed several times also during other projects presented in this case about which I testified in November 2013. I used the integrated mortality database which was a source for cross-referencing the records of the missing and checking whether the reporting of the disappearance is consistently reported there as well and to exclude the possibility that someone has survived Tomasica, but they didn't, or were confirmed dead. What else I used?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What reliability factor? You told what you use, I believe, in your report. I'm asking for a reliability factor for, for instance, the 1991 census and the integrated mortality database which you just mentioned? Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I again cannot give you a single number on the scale from one to ten, for example, because I don't have such a scale. But as I'm saying, census, for example, 1991 census, even though it has its problems, it's a very useful source for checking -- improving the validity of the reporting by other sources. Well, we as the demographic unit invested a lot of time and effort to eliminate mistakes from the census and improve the reporting of the names in the census. It took us several years until we established a version that could be reliably used in our work, and honestly I believe it is a very reliable source of information, very reliable source of information that proved to be helping me to make decisions about many things, like, you know, matching on the first place, consistency of lists, places of residence, places of disappearance, ethnicity, age, many, many, many, many aspects that I studied in my reports. Integrated database is a very large database that is a complication of several sources --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How reliable is it, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my eyes, very reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could please turn to page 13 of your Tomasica report in English, and it will be page 16 in the B/C/S, and I want to look at table number 4. Now, if I've done my arithmetic correctly, I think we have 327 total Tomasica remains of males that fall between the ages of 15 years to 64 years. Would you agree with me that this represents over 91 per cent of all the remains of males?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the specific figures in front of my eyes, but this sounds very correct to me. There may be slight differences, but, yeah, that is what it says, actually, in my report in the paragraph just above the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to 1D1235, while we wait for it, I can introduce it as a decree with the force of law of defence of the RBiH Presidency promulgated 20 May 1992. And if we can have Article 51 of the same, found on page 3 of the B/C/S, page 18 of the English. And it says here: "All citizens between 15 and 60 (men) or 55 (women) have the right and obligation to train for defence if fit to attend training." First of all, Dr. Tabeau, did you have occasion to review this document or any document like it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that this means that a significant portion of the 91 per cent of the remains that were males between the ages of 14 and 60 were within the age group with an obligation to defend their country and to report for training?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, is there any dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: About the content of this document? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No? About -- the question whether there's any dispute about this legislation means that a significant portion of the 91 per cent of the remains were males within the age group with an obligation to defend their country and to report for training. Mr. Ivetic, I'm just wondering why we need a witness to say this. If the law says between 15 and 64, and if we have a table, then our own logic would give the answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But neither you nor I prepared this report. Dr. Tabeau did. And I'm asking about what she took into account when she did her report and how reliable it is for us to make determinations from the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, she told us that she didn't look at that legislation and then you followed up to ask for the obvious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to take a look at 1D5477. And I can introduce it as follows: This was used as an exhibit in the Tadic case, and for some reason page 2 is the English of the title. And after we see the title -- so if we can have page 1 on the right, page 2 on the left, we'll have both languages of the title of this document. And it says: "List of Mobilisation." And now if we can turn to page 3, we'll see a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 3 which language?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's all one language, Your Honours -- pardon me, it's not all one language. It's all one document with multiple languages. However, the lists of names have not been translated or were not translated when this was used in a prior case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My first question to you, madam: We see here the words TO BiH and Sto Kozarac. In your years of work at the OTP, would you agree with me that the abbreviations TO often refer to the entity known as the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by the way, was this a document that you may have looked at for purposes of your Tomasica review?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me Kozarac is a region contained in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any dispute about where Kozarac is?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Defence has not had time to do an exhaustive demographic search, but we did find a total of 18 persons listed as exhumed from Tomasica whose names match one or more names on this mobilisation list of the Territorial Defence of the BiH from Kozarac in Prijedor. Does that result surprise you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am surprised that you compare just the first name and surname, you know. In this case, what kind of comparison is this? If you would have compared more information, like including father's name and date of birth at least, then you could have obtained first a much more reliable result and much fewer matches. Well, it is still and will remain just a mobilisation list which doesn't say anything about whether they died as combatants, in combat, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't recall asking about that. I asked if you were surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would the witness be surprised of, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The results. That there were matches, potential matches between the names of Tomasica victims and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you're -- the first surprise the witness mentioned was that you used this data for comparison purposes. And then indeed she went on to say which is apparently not part of what you consider to be surprises. Perhaps if you put specific questions to the witness, we might move on in a more efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, madam, as a demographer if you were presented with this list looking on the right-hand side, would you agree with me that the only type of matching I could have done with this list was with the names since that's all that's listed in there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can match a telephone book with the victims list from Tomasica, but what is the meaning of that? So the matching process must remain meaningful. First it has to be meaningful and then it has to be possible. So in this case, I don't see it meaningful and I don't see it really taking you where you want to be because the information on the list is extremely limited. That is all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me without access to your keys, your results are just as meaningless?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not about the keys. It is about the content of this list. It is about the information available. It is about what you can match with other lists --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that other sources beyond this one document should be checked to find out if these and other names of Tomasica bodies may have been engaged as members of an armed force prior to their death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean engaged in the factual terms of -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would not exclude those who were, though mobilised, would be at home or at work or -- the one doesn't exclude the other, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not talking about combat. I'm just talking about being mobilised as members of an armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said "engaged."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an armed force. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I tried to further specify so as to assist the witness in answering the question as understood by you as the examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I would kindly ask Mr. Ivetic to help. Is it a list of mobilised or to be mobilised people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a long document, Your Honours. And for many of the lists -- it's different lists from different areas, and some of the lists have signatures of individuals next to their names, so in that sense I would assume, but my assumption doesn't mean that it's actually the case, but I would assume if they signed the list next to their name that they accepted to be mobilised into that force. But that's not what I want to ask Ms. Tabeau, but that does address I think the gist of your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's now get back to the question. Perhaps you repeat it, Mr. Ivetic, so that the witness now having understood some of the issues involved in the question itself can answer and let's see whether she can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that other sources beyond this one document should be checked to find out if these and other names of Tomasica victims may be matched with persons who were mobilised as members of an armed force prior to their deaths.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the lists of mobilised persons, I don't feel they take me anywhere as I said already, you know, because if my purpose would be to distinguish between combatants and non-combatants, I would have to go and study the circumstances of the deaths in terms other than the causes of death that are available here for the Tomasica victims, and I'm afraid I didn't have such sources at my disposal. I could have marked individuals on the Tomasica list as being army members or not, but it would still don't give me the answer about dying in combat or dying not in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you've told us that you followed the same methodology as in your Srebrenica report, but you will recall for purposes of your Srebrenica report you yourself wrote several Request for Assistance to the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina to determine if members -- persons on that list were members of their armed forces. Even following the methodology, did you do that at all for these Tomasica listed victims?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do that for Tomasica victims, but I could do that and I can still provide a list very easily if you wish so, but it still doesn't answer the question about dieing in combat and dying not in combat. In Srebrenica cases, as you yourself remember, a distinction was made between persons listed on the -- in the army records and not. Yet the essential part of the victims' analysis are the exhumation records, are the sites, whether they were mass graves, and what the on-site investigation tells about the links of the sites with certain incidents that led to deaths of individuals buried in the sites. So you could be listed, what I'm trying to say, as a soldier on an army list or mobilisation list, but it doesn't tell you about how the person really died.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you think it would not be interesting information for purposes of testing conclusions of other people as to how and when they died?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was tasked to provide an analysis that would tell about the number of victims buried in Tomasica. That is what I did. Certainly I could have done more, many more things. I can myself think of several excellent ideas to expand on in the very same report. I was also tasked to investigate the context of how these people disappeared, which I did. And this is all I was tasked with and I was not crossing these mandates, if I may call it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now just so I can understand your answer at line 19, page 73, you said: "I didn't do that for Tomasica victims, but I could do that and I can still provide a list very easily..." Am I to understand that you do have information and a list as to members of the army that are to be found in the Tomasica list or please -- help me explain what you just said?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could provide it easily but doesn't mean that I do have it and I looked into it and I studied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have it as part of the system of the population databases which I used for this report. So if there is an order from -- from this Court for me to do so, I can of course provide such a list which still is beyond the tasks that were -- that I was told to do for this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can return to your report, and I apologise, I think that is P7449, and if we could turn to page 23 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S. In the English, it will be the second paragraph from the top; on the B/C/S, it will be the third paragraph from the bottom. And I quote now: "It is indeed possible, extensively and comprehensively possible, to prove that both many whole bodies and many fragmented body parts, those from Tomasica, as well as those from Jakarina Kosa, were subject of shooting from machine or sometimes handguns ..." Dr. Tabeau, you earlier used the word "execution" in describing what you believed happened to these individuals. Is this one of the bases upon which you concluded that these bodies were the result of execution?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you just read is, indeed, a quote from my report which I made based on my studying the report of Clark and his report of causes of death. So that's the foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you happen in your work to get a copy or consider Bruno Franjic's ballistics report of disputed cartridges and bullet rounds found in the Tomasica grave and removed from bodies of victims during autopsy?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't study this report and I didn't use any evidence from that report in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be surprised, Dr. Tabeau, to find out that Mr. Franjic was unable to conclusively identify any of the bullets from Tomasica as having come from a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer must be I don't know simply because I'm not familiar with his report and his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to take a look at Dr. Clark's report; P7433, page 8 in the English, page 10 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, while this is coming up, could I also ask Mr. Ivetic for a reference to the parts of Mr. Franjic report that he cited to or referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The entire report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, no, no. The line or page reference for the conclusion that you read to Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Every conclusion in the report could not conclude -- could not conclude machine-guns. In court when I suggested machine-guns, Mr. Franjic disputed and said, no, no, they could not have come from machine-guns. I can get it for you at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we now, have at least one half of the ... Is this Dr. Clark's report? It does not look like it to me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you kindly repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 7433 is the number I have written down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 7433 is the curriculum vitae of Mr. Bruno Franjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Clark's report is marked with the number P7443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look and see whether -- what appears is his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could turn to page 8 in the English, page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in here, we have from Dr. Clark that most injuries were from high-velocity weapons. And if we turn to page 13 in the English, page 16 in the B/C/S, and it's the first line in the English, and Dr. Clark concludes: "The vast majority of gun-shot injuries seen in the Tomasica cases appear to have been caused by bullets fired from high-velocity rifles," with a definite or suggestive use of handguns in 23 instances. Dr. Tabeau, would you agree that Dr. Clark in his report never mentioned machine-guns. That's something that you inserted into the analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You forget about the two long lists that go together with this report. In order to say yes or no, I would have to search through this list and come back with the answer whether the word "machine" was used in these annexes. It must have come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Dr. Clark uses "high-velocity rifle." I put it to you that word is not found in your report. Why?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that Ms. Tabeau must use the language of some other people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If she claims she is relying upon their conclusions to draw conclusions of her own, I think she does have to accurately quote the terminology of other people and understand what that terminology means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When she said "machine-gun," was she quoting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She just said she was relying upon Dr. Clark. That's where my confusion lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Relying upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- what the witness said is that she would like to inspect the annexes so as to find out whether her quote "machine-guns" find its basis there. Now that Dr. Clark uses the expression "high-velocity rifles," I think it was, or "high-velocity weapons," that doesn't affect that, and I do not know whether this witness would not agree with that or contradict that because Dr. Clark says a large majority, which leaves a minority over, and I do not know whether at this moment we're looking at the minority cases which are left or whether we are talking about the overall majority conclusions. Let's keep that very --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am keeping that in mind, but Dr. Tabeau's words are it is indeed possible, extensively and comprehensively possible, to prove that both many whole bodies and many fragmented body parts, so she's definitely talking many, not the minority. Am I correct, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the simple answer is I'm happy to search through these annexes of Mr. Clark and see whether the term was used and in how many instances. It is also possible, as I am not an expert in ballistics, that I mix-up terms and misinterpreted something, but before I agree I did I would like to run this search.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with you running that search on your own time, but we have to keep going with questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So perhaps, Your Honours, I don't know if at the next break the report could be provided to the witness by VWS. I've no problem with her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the annexes could be provided to the witness during the break, which we'll start now as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that I have to go back to my office to search electronically, very quickly. I can be assisted in doing that with somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on whether any of the parties has problems with you seeking assistance and going back to your office which is, if I understand well, located within the OTP premises. I leave it to Mr. Ivetic at this moment to express whether or not he has any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If she remains in the presence of the Court usher, I don't see a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want the court usher to accompany her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would that be the procedure for a witness who is on the stand, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that's -- Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, we wouldn't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection whatsoever. If the Registry has no objection that the court usher accompanies Ms. Tabeau to her office and looks into her computer, I take it that the usher is not in a position to check exactly what Ms. Tabeau is doing on her computer but we leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The usher is just to ensure no one else talks to Dr. Tabeau. That's what I understand it as. It's just so that no one else interferes with the witness. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier Ms. Tabeau you said that you would need the assistance of another person. Can you do it without that other person so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the assistance of usher I meant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that somebody is just keeping an eye on me to be sure that I don't do anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- wrong. That is exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would 20 minutes be approximately enough to search for the machine-guns in the annexes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 2.00. And Ms. Tabeau will be accompanied by the usher. But could the witness first leave the courtroom. She's in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for Dr. Tabeau I can give my colleagues on the other side the citations from Mr. Franjic's report to look at. It's Exhibit P7435, pages 102 through 111, and Exhibit P7434, pages 47 to 50 where he does all the opinions as to the cartridges, and I think everyone will agree he's not able to conclusively identify a machine-gun for any of them. And at transcript page 36501 to 36502 he took issue from me even suggesting a machine-gun based upon different characteristics on the cartridges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you remind the number of cartridges which he compared was approximately what? Was that less than the number of bodies or main cases that were found or was it more?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think he examined something in the realm of 18 cartridges and some rounds of which most of the rounds he was not able to perform an analysis of, but I don't have -- I don't have the -- recall for the actual numbers, but I would suspect to be less than the bodies. That's my general impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Your Honours, we will check those references because our recollection is that the witness didn't rule out completely the possibility, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I take it you had a safe trip to your office and a safe trip back again. Could you report on anything you may have found during this break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I searched through both annexes Clark provided for three terms, "machine," separately "gun," then separately "velocity" in any context in any part of the phrases on several data items. "Machine," the word "machine" does not appear there. The word "gun" appears in the context of handgun shots in a number of cases but not in a large number of cases. The "velocity" appears in the context of high-velocity and it appears in very many cases. Actually, 283 cases the word "high-velocity" has been used. Well, going back to my statement in the report and using the term "machine-gun," I certainly misinterpreted the word "high-velocity" for machine-gun. I'm not an expert in ballistics, and I wouldn't be able to explain all the differences between these two, so it is my reading of high-velocity gun-shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have interpreted high-velocity as the frequency of shots being fired rather than the speed of the projectile. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I most likely did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, a little bit earlier you in response to my questions talked about the tasking that you received for this report. From whom did you -- pardon me. Did you receive your tasking from the Office of the Prosecutor orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From whom did receive your assignments and/or tasking from the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Camille Bibles, previously the Senior Trial Attorney on the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to talk about something you said last week. But before we do, I would like to talk about your slideshow presentation that we saw in court these last few days. Why did you wait until a day or two before your testimony to complete and disclose the same to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, first of all, I finished it the day before the testimony, and, actually, I insisted to have a presentation of this type as I find it helps not only me but everybody else in the courtroom to go through it, whereas, well, the idea was not very easily accommodated by the attorneys who were taking me in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know that the Defence was granted one month of time to prepare for the Tomasica reopening?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not watching the court proceedings every day but I know there is a limit. And if you say you had one month, it was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to that which I want to ask you about, and it was at transcript page 36745 where you were asked by Judge Orie as follows, and this was -- pardon me, this was in relation to slide 14 of your preparation by the way: "JUDGE ORIE: Yes, and you wouldn't know. So when you said the number for Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje are not complete, they may be complete, they may not be complete. Is that -- "THE WITNESS: That is my understanding too. They may be but more likely incomplete." The question I have for you Dr. Tabeau: What is the demographic bases on which you conclude that these numbers for these locations more likely are incomplete when Judge Orie is correct and you agree with him that the two are equally valid options -- that there are two equally valid options that exist?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, strictly speaking Judge Orie is, of course, right. They might be complete, they might be incomplete. I don't know that. However, from the -- my experience as I read the reports on the missing persons, I see that what is reported there is the location, people, the victims were last seen, last seen. Further, some people could have gone to camps like Keraterm or Omarska and they saw certain relatives for the last time there, but most people reported, rather, the places where they lived, the small villages where they saw their relatives for the last time. So I believe that in order to provide correct numbers of individuals who were, in fact, last seen, really, could have been last seen, really, in the camps, it be would higher numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: In relation to the camps and into the events in Prijedor, do you believe in the Prosecution's case as to what happened to ethnic Muslims and ethnic Croats?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question? I don't understand the question really.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Prosecution case is right? Do you believe in the Prosecution's case, their theory as to what happened to people that in Prijedor including in these three locations, Keraterm Omarska, and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the Prosecution thinks of these camps, but I know what I have shown in the report, so what I know is in the report. There were people reported disappeared from the camps. And I provided you with these numbers, and these are in my opinion minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you in your work at the Office of the Prosecutor either in this stint or the original stint have a role in advising the Office of the Prosecution as to how to phrase their case as to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this say, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to and review the Prosecution witness testimony or statements as to Prijedor, Omarska, Keraterm, and/or Trnopolje while doing your work?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm trying to skip through some of my questions. By the way, if we can back to the I think it was seven sources that you consulted for your Tomasica report. How many of these sources do you consider as a demographer contained reliable confirmation of the death of individuals?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the source that is -- that offers a confirmation of the deaths and -- of the individuals is the ICMP DNA match reports that simply confirm that these people who at some point were reported missing were buried in Tomasica and identified as the actual deaths. Of course, on the top of it or in addition to this we have the 600 approximately documents from the BH prosecutor office that directly also go into the death details of these individuals. So the rest would be the missing persons records and of course Clark's records of the post-mortem investigation was definitely confirmed, the deaths of these people, although there are no names there associated with the cases. So it would be ICMP, Clark, the BH prosecutor's documents that confirm the deaths. On the top of it, there is the disappearance information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn to 1D5784. While we wait for that, I'll tell you this is an excerpt from the UN statistics division demographic year book showing historic data from 1948 to 1997 for various countries. Did you consult such data or such a source for purposes of any of your demographic work for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't read it because letters are very -- extremely small, but it would be probably the deaths, records of the dead people, right, by age and then sex and urban and rural divide, et cetera, et cetera. The thing is, Mr. Ivetic, that these are known deaths, not the missing persons record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I'm simply asking did you review these?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because I wouldn't find the Tomasica victims in aggregate statistics or known deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, we have data 1989 and 1990 for Bosnia-Herzegovina showing for both years approximately 30.000 in deaths. Now would you agree with me based upon the years covered by these figures, that these 30.000 approximate deaths per year had nothing to do with ethnic cleansing or the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is probably depending on the year. It is a long number of years that are shown here in this slide, but the -- United Nations division in New York certainly provides statistics in normal times, not in the time of war. So it is not what they can compile, the deaths and missing persons in the time of war. Whether it was 30.000 a year or slightly more, I don't know exactly and we don't see it on the slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do see something. I think the total number for 1989, as far as I can see, is a little bit over 30.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's for Bosnia-Herzegovina, apparently. And then 1990 is 29.000, a little bit over that. And the question by Mr. Ivetic was whether this is related to the war circumstances? Mr. Ivetic, is there a suggestion in your question that in 1989 and 1990 there was already a war ongoing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I was asking for Dr. Tabeau to be on the same page as me and confirm that these are not war-related because they predate the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So if you have any reason to change that understanding, Ms. Tabeau -- then apparently not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree in peacetime, or normal time I think you called it just a few moments ago, cause of death can be due to old age, accident, and ordinary criminal homicide that is not related to war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you asking for the obvious, Mr. Ivetic? Do we need an expert to tell us that people can die from natural causes? Do we need an expert to tell us that people can die from old age or from criminal homicide? Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Tabeau, 30.000 persons a year times the four years of the war between 1992 and 1995 by my math would project an approximation of 120.000 people who would have died of causes unrelated to the war during those years. Demographically speaking am I write?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a simple extrapolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can tender this document as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you if elderly people would die from natural causes, is there a possibility - and I'm asking you - that they would not die from those natural causes but would die as a result of war? They may have died otherwise for by other purposes. So when you said, yes, of course, is there anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, well, it is -- this kind of projection for four years ahead, the years that were war years in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that does not make any sense, of course, at all. First of all, people who would have died in normal time of old age, accidents, criminal violence, would have died of war-related causes, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some of them [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them, not all of them. Of course, some of them. So there would be a total different pattern of dying in this period, so making an extrapolation of 30.000 over four years of war is not the way to come up with a number of deaths in the war time. So there will be both types of deaths. There will be deaths of old age, diseases, accidents, and criminal violence, but there will be also other deaths, war-related deaths of both civilians and soldiers that would change the pattern of dying during the war time completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said "yes, of course" in view of the question, you meant to say something different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the simple extrapolation cannot be made in a -- in a way that makes sense because people might have still died from natural causes or old age, whereas others may have been caught by a bullet in combat situations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. That is what I meant. So extrapolation is a process that is based on certain assumptions, and one can extrapolate, of course, but the meaning of such an extrapolation is simply zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the question, therefore, the question was that if 30.000 people in a non-war situation would die from natural causes or from criminal activities, whether you would expect between 1992 and 1994, in four years, 120.000 people would have died, of course, is unrelated to the war. There is not a clear yes to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the 120 could have been expected for normal time. If there were no war, one could think of extrapolating and using the regular assumptions. If -- I don't know, demographer would probably extrapolate or most likely extrapolate like that, but that is all what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question included what would be the situation during four years of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I missed that. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I tendered the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1091, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just quickly look at 1D5783.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This again from the United Nations statistical department, the demography handbook published in 2006, and in this excerpt if we turn to page 10, I think here we'll see data for various European encounters from 2002 through 2006. And if we zoom in, hopefully we'll Bosnia near the top of the list. And for Bosnia for these years, we see the deaths include death rates and we see 30.000 up, up, all the way up until 34.000 for one year. And first of all, madam, given this pattern both before and after the war of approximately 30.000 deaths due to a variety of causes not related to the war, can we conclude that a significant number of persons died during the war of causes not related to the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, what can you conclude about the war if the war is not part of this slide that we have on our screen and wasn't part of the previous slide? So these are two slides that are unrelated. In the meantime, the population size have changed. It was 4.4 million of individuals in Bosnia. Then at some point it was 3.5 million. So there was census not that long ago that shows the changes in the population size. In the meantime, the age structure of the population changed as well, as all populations, also the Bosnian population ages, so from a smaller population we still can end with 30.000 deaths a year of [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention an amount. Just so you understand my question, are you now telling us that you exclude the possibility that there were a certain number or a certain percentage of the population during the war years that died of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never said I exclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people die of natural causes also in the war time, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we don't know that number, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not exactly. We know some of these numbers but not exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we return -- first of all, let's tender this as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1092, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to your report, P7449, and look at page 30 in English and the corresponding page will be 38 in the B/C/S. Now, here is the beginning of your section dealing with Prijedor and the ARK. And here you analyse, according to the bullet points: How many missing persons were there from Prijedor in 1992, who went missing from Prijedor, what's their age, sex, ethnicity, what major disappearance events can be seen in the records of the missing from Prijedor. Would you agree with me that for all four of these questions in this report you, and when I say "you" I mean your office at the Office of the Prosecutor, had in its possession the data and information at your disposal long before the Tomasica evidence came into light and long before the reopening was sought.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sources, ICRC list and Prijedor Book of Missing, were indeed in possession of the OTP for a long time, and analysis of Prijedor missing were made in the past. I mentioned today in this court that I made some studies on this in the past. What was done now was a reassessment of the missing from Prijedor and the ARK region, including the latest version of the ICRC list in the reassessment and producing the statistics as I mentioned in the bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Doctor. Two of your reports deal with municipalities in Prijedor - they're P2798 and P2796 in evidence - but would you agree with me that this type of analysis linking Prijedor missing persons to incidents from the indictment was never performed in those reports even though you had that data in your possession as to non-Tomasica victims long before the Prosecution rested its case in 2013?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was indeed the case that in the past the proof of death analysis wasn't done the same way as it is done these days. I think that my personal experience and also the experience of my former unit has grown over the years, and the focus recently has been much more the POD analysis, proof of death analysis. So what can I say? It is just where we ended, and, yeah, that is what I had done in other cases recently was also now down for Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me this Tomasica report was intended to supplement and fill a hole that had been left in your reports as to Prijedor that we talked about in November of 2013?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was intended. It was my decision to make this report the way I made it. I thought it really very important to made it in this way. I didn't have any intention of, you know, supplementing or not supplementing. I was thinking of what is needed and what I thought was important to do in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, could I ask you the following. Looking at the items Mr. Ivetic did put to you, was it at the time possible to link missing persons to persons that would have deceased, especially in relation to those persons identified after the -- after revealing the Tomasica mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously we didn't have the identifications of the Tomasica victims, so this type of analysis was simply not possible sooner than I made it for Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have identifications for Jakarina Kosa?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Jakarina Kosa, yes, there were identifications. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you could have done this analysis earlier for Jakarina Kosa in 2013?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that many of the Jakarina Kosa identifications are included in the POD annex that I made earlier in November 2013 I testified about -- [Overlapping speakers] ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. And none of them are linked to incidents from the indictment; isn't that correct? You waited until now to do that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not correct. Like, the POD annex speak to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're now giving an answer apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can object to a question but you can't give what you consider to be the right answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Then I object to the question as not correctly characterising the content of P2797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, to the extent possible, but it's always a bit problematic if we're talking about the negative, what was not done, but if -- but perhaps we should leave that until tomorrow. If you could phrase your question again tomorrow clearly indicating from where it becomes clear that a certain link was not considered or established by the witness in a previous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, either given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 8th of July, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of July, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
